One promising application is translating natural-language questions into SPARQL (text-to-SPARQL), which would let building operators query these graphs through language agents, but progress is limited by the scarcity of large natural-language/SPARQL benchmarks. This paper presents Build2SPARQL, a large-scale benchmark for building KGs generated by a KG-grounded pipeline: SPARQL queries are produced and validated entirely by graph-traversal code, while large language models generate only the natural-language questions, keeping query correctness independent of model behavior. The pipeline mines six query-pattern families -- linear chains, branching, UNION, aggregation, OPTIONAL, and attribute-filtered -- and phrases each query across five vocabulary registers. Applied to 201 building KGs (180 Brick, 21 ASHRAE 223P), it yields 6,136 executable SPARQL queries and 30,680 questions. A two-rater human validation of 300 questions found 98.8% semantic fidelity, 98.8% naturalness, and 84.0% operational plausibility. A retrieval-augmented evaluation across three open-weight language models raised exact-match accuracy from 0.2-20% (zero-shot) to 56-65% (three-shot retrieved).

2610.04012.title: Beyond the Parameter Monolith: Reconstructive Memories, Executable Skills, and Residual Assembly for Language Models
2610.04012.abstract: Can a language-model system grow its external state and use executable procedures without making every component part of one shared optimization process? We present FEM-ASM, an implemented architecture that separates neural coordination, document-state construction, and deterministic execution. Independent workers optimize document memories under a frozen codec and publish immutable, versioned artifacts. Executable skills return bounded computation results. Both enter a shared neural field through type-specific adapters, explicit support mappings, and a common residual-assembly operator. The resulting computation couples a quadratic consistency substep to a recurrent learned correction. We evaluate memory construction, controlled retrieval, positional readout, execution-result rendering, and evidence attachment with unchanged core weights. The experiments show that recoverable storage, successful retrieval, and successful neural use are distinct properties. Position-specific observations improve the tested memory and execution-result interfaces, while fixed-core attachment demonstrates that newly available evidence can affect predictions through the existing interface. The contribution is an architectural and engineering account of independently produced state participating in shared neural computation, with explicit component contracts, executable protocols, and released research artifacts.

2610.04188.title: Agentic AI with Structured CoT for Enhancing AI's Spatial Intelligence: Visualization and Reasoning of Rotation
2610.04188.abstract: Recent studies show that artificial intelligence (AI) with language and vision capabilities still experiences limitations in spatial reasoning. In this paper, we have studied the spatial capabilities of advanced generative AI to understand the rotations of objects in 3D space, utilizing AI's image processing and language processing features. We trained and examined the spatial intelligence of a generative Agentic AI model (GPT-5.6) to understand the spatial rotation process with rotation diagrams based on the revised Purdue Spatial Visualization Test: Visualization of Rotations (Revised PSVT:R). We improvised the Revised PSVT:R by superimposing additional graphical and contextual features to evaluate how different Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning strategies influence model performance. The results indicate that structured CoT reasoning improves the spatial reasoning performance of the base GPT-5.6 model in both datasets (PSVT:R and PSVT:R with coordinate system). We used three CoT approaches - (1) Structured CoT, (2) few-shot Structured CoT, and Structured CoT with Self-optimized Prompt. The three CoT approaches evaluated in this study showed no significant performance difference. Results showed that combining structured CoT reasoning with relevant contextual information leads to considerable improvements in VLM performance on 3D rotation tasks, demonstrating the potential of agentic AI for more effective spatial reasoning. However, when contextual information is removed, structured CoT reasoning alone provides limited improvement, and the models continue to exhibit notable difficulties in understanding spatial transformations. These findings suggest that effective spatial reasoning in VLMs relies on the integration of visual, textual, and reasoning-based information in future agentic AI systems for spatial intelligence.

2610.05162.title: Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy
2610.05162.authors: Ruqing Ning, Haibo Meng, Zhishang Xiang, Zerui Chen, Jinsong Su, Xin Wang, Qinggang Zhang
2610.05162.abstract: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

2610.08586.title: MINDSET: Energy-based Memory Evolution for Long Conversational Agents
2610.08586.authors: Sujato Dutta, Sreekruthy Tummala, Shashank Vanga, Ayushmi Pavani, BHVSP Subrahmanyam, Neeraj Choudhary
2610.08586.abstract: Long-term conversational memory requires more than retrieving past dialogue. A system must determine whether new evidence replaces an existing fact, applies in a different context or represents an unresolved contradiction. We introduce MINDSET, a local memory controller that makes these decisions without any LLM calls. It preserves original dialogue episodes and organizes them into provenance-linked, versioned schemas. For each incoming episode, a feasibility-constrained energy objective governs four possible transitions: reinforcement, supersession, contextual branching and new-schema creation. Stability rules prevent isolated conflicts from prematurely displacing established states while version links preserve access to historical evidence. At inference time, retrieval follows these structures back to original dialogue. On a frozen 700-question LoCoMo subset, MINDSET achieves the highest observed answer F1 among six evaluated systems and significantly improves retrieval ranking. Without retuning, it achieves the highest judge accuracy on LongMemEval knowledge-update cases, compared with the other baselines evaluated. Additional experiments with GLM-4.7 and Gemma-4-31B demonstrate compatibility across answer backbones. These results support explicit, non-generative memory-state control as an effective approach to address evolving conversational knowledge.

2610.09142.title: Finding Side-Effect Loopholes in AppWorld and WorkArena Verifiers
2610.09142.abstract: Language-model agents act for people inside software, sending payments or editing records. Benchmarks such as AppWorld and WorkArena grade them with automated verifiers, whose verdicts also become reinforcement learning (RL) rewards, so a lenient verifier rewards mistakes. Verifier audits mostly hunt for runs that pass without doing the task; we ask about runs that do it and also change something nobody asked for. We mutation-test both verifiers with hand-written edits to correct runs, designed from the verifier source; an end-state check confirms each false positive. All confirmed false positives were unrequested changes; planted omissions and wrong values produced none. AppWorld's tests passed a duplicate write in all six tasks of two templates, and three RL methods that train on one of these templates would fully reward it; one count assertion per template rejected all six duplicates while passing every correct run. WorkArena's form verifier, called once after submission, passed all 36 edited runs that filled an unrequested field. Checked after every field, it caught extra fields filled first or in drop-downs but still passed all 8 runs that filled a text or reference field last. Both verifiers check that the requested change happened but not reliably that nothing else changed.

2610.18449.title: Autonomous Science Bench: Evaluating AI Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
2610.18449.abstract: AI agents for autonomous scientific discovery must decide which experiments to run under a limited budget. Most benchmarks for science agents provide fixed datasets, while others that support active experimentation largely rely on simulation. We introduce Autonomous Science Bench, an initial release comprising six budgeted design-build-test-learn campaigns grounded in published experiments across biology, chemistry, and materials science. Agents select batches of designs, receive measurements from a lab service, and use the results to guide subsequent experiments before delivering a predictive model. Success requires passing two calibrated gates: a discovery gate, which evaluates the designs the agent measured, and a learning gate, which evaluates its model's ranking of held-out designs. In a pilot evaluation of ten agent-model configurations and 180 trials, the best configuration succeeds in 72% of trials, while the hardest campaign is solved in only five of 30 attempts. The two gates reveal different weaknesses: some agents build accurate rankings but find too few promising designs, while others find promising designs but fail to predict which unseen designs will perform well. These differences are obscured by overall success rates alone. We release version 0.1 of the campaigns, lab runtime, and public leaderboard at https://asb.open-ssi.org/.

2610.22872.title: Look Back, Correct Forward: Error Feedback Calibration for Time Series Forecasting
2610.22872.authors: Haonan Yang, Yulin He, Zhuo Li, Jing Zhao, Huibin Tan
2610.22872.abstract: Time series forecasting models are increasingly deployed in continuously evolving environments. After a forecast is issued, future observations gradually arrive and reveal how the model has failed. Existing methods mainly treat such observations as supervision for parameter updates. However, it remains unclear whether verified forecasting errors can themselves provide causal feedback for correcting future predictions. To address this, we introduce Error Feedback Calibration (EFC), a fully test-time framework for deterministic post-hoc correction of time series forecasting. EFC constructs a Causal Error Diagonal (CED) from revealed errors of overlapping historical forecasts, providing a fresh view of the frozen forecaster's recent failure behavior. Then Cumulative Error Transport (CET) maps this error state to future residuals using cumulative estimation, while temporal out-of-sample validation controls the correction strength. Temporal Residual Learning (TRL) further predicts only the residual structure left after CET from recent CED trajectories, rather than relearning the entire forecasting error. Extensive experiments across forecasting backbones and datasets show that EFC broadly improves forecasting performance while substantially controlling harmful over correction.

2610.26430.title: Physiology-Aware Graph Attention for Early Ventricular Reentry Prediction
2610.26430.authors: Ma{\"e}lis Morier (EPIONE), Jairo Rodr{\'i}guez Padilla (IHU-LIRYC), Mihaela Pop (ISIR, MLIA), Patrick Gallinari (ISIR, MLIA), Maxime Sermesant (EPIONE)
2610.26430.abstract: Sudden cardiac death mostly originates from post-infarct ventricular tachycardia. This reentry is sustained by propagation around scar tissue, but its risk remains difficult to predict from infarct imaging alone. While in silico induction studies can reveal these mechanisms, exploring many substrates and pacing locations remains computationally expensive. We propose a graph attention classifier for early prediction of sustained ventricular reentry from simulated cardiac electrophysiology. Each simulation is represented as a graph with early nodal voltage samples and edge attributes encoding geometry, stimulation frequency, tissue labels, amplitude, and diastolic interval. These descriptors are computed only from the first two paced activations, before sustained reentry is observed. On a balanced independent test set of 1000 simulations, the classifier achieves 94.6% accuracy, 95.4% sensitivity, 93.8% specificity, 94.6% F1-score, 0.987 ROC-AUC, and 0.985 PR-AUC. Ablation experiments show that diastolic interval is the most critical descriptor. Qualitative attention inspection suggests that different heads focus on border-zone, stimulation location, and early propagation path. These results support graph attention as a fast early-prediction approach for large-scale in silico ventricular reentry studies.

2610.28537.title: Beyond 4 bits: Data-Centric Post-training Quantization and Recovery
2610.28537.authors: Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker, Riccardo Grazzi, James Hensman, Pashmina Cameron
2610.28537.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with a limited compute and data budget. Down to 4 bits, state-of-the-art PTQ methods are near-lossless; below this limit, the tested scalar PTQ configurations collapse to near-random accuracy and quality becomes acutely sensitive to choices such as the quantization representation and calibration data. At such low bitwidths, recovery fine-tuning becomes crucial, and its effectiveness depends heavily on these same choices. Yet there is little systematic evidence on how the quantization method, the quality and task alignment of calibration data, and the design of the recovery procedure interact to determine the final 2-bit model. We present a systematic study of 2-bit quantization and recovery fine-tuning across model families, scales, and data distributions, and distill our findings into practical, architecture-dependent best practices for obtaining an accurate 2-bit model. This recipe, which combines a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and a short codebook-only distillation stage, restores 63-68% average accuracy across seven question-answering tasks at 2 bits (a 71-73% BF16 ceiling), versus the near-random 29% of the evaluated scalar PTQ pipelines, at roughly half the compute of a full-model QAT baseline. Given the same calibration and recovery data, EfficientQAT, a trained scalar baseline, avoids the collapse. However, at a matched rate it trails the vector recipe on generation on every model (2.8-10.9 AvgGen; within noise on Qwen3-MoE) and on question answering on three of the four studied models (2.7-7.8 AvgQA). We also find that the best recovery data depends on the calibration data, an interaction confirmed on a held-out model. Our architecture-aware map of the 2-bit design space shows that representation, calibration data, and recovery data must be chosen jointly.

2610.29271.title: ARCANA: A Benchmark for Abstraction and Analogical Reasoning
2610.29271.authors: Ruqi Chen, Zilei Wang, Wei Wang
2610.29271.abstract: Analogical reasoning is widely considered a fundamental component of human intelligence. Few benchmarks are designed to explicitly test far analogical reasoning - reasoning between domains that are superficially dissimilar yet share deep relational or structural similarities. In this work, we introduce an analogical reasoning benchmark called Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus of ANAlogy (ARCANA). The tasks of ARCANA require performing far analogical mappings from real-world objects or physical phenomena to abstract grid-based transformations, different from the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark which primarily emphasized innate human priors. We validate ARCANA through a human study, demonstrating that humans solve these tasks reliably. In contrast, evaluations across a range of large language models show a distinct performance gap compared to humans, revealing systematic failure modes that remain challenging for current models. To address this gap, we propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection. Experiments demonstrate that ConceptSIR enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that were unsolved by direct prompting in our evaluation. Overall, our results suggest that far analogical reasoning remains an open problem for contemporary LLMs. All the materials are available at sites.google.com/view/arcanacogtest. The complete codebase, including benchmark, and ConceptSIR, is publicly available at https://github.com/density-11/arcana-test. All ARCANA data and task instances can be accessed and explored at https://arcanacogtest.org/.

2610.32110.title: Who Verifies the Tools? How Warped Formatters Mislead Agents and Their Verifiers
2610.32110.abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool did. We saw such misrepresentations in a production RAG research system used by the Pilsudski Institute in New York, where tool output formatters misled an agent into giving wrong or incomplete information to users. Each tool did its job correctly, but its output omitted search limits, result caps, or identifier namespaces. Within this same production system, we studied whether faulty formatters mislead agents and verifiers and how much repaired wording helps. We fed tool results to agents using two formatter versions: one with key omissions and one with all missing details clearly stated. That difference alone changed what the agents claimed and what the verifiers accepted. Unsupported agent claims dropped substantially for three of the four failure types. In one test, verifiers went from accepting incorrect answers 90 out of 90 times to rejecting them 90 out of 90 times. A control showed the verifiers could catch the errors once they were given the missing facts and asked to judge correctness. We include the audit prompt we used with Codex and Claude Code in an exploratory demonstration, written with prior knowledge of our own system's defects. When pointed at an old version of our own system, it rediscovered the defects that were still live and surfaced twelve more we had not catalogued. When pointed at OpenClaw and Hermes, two of the best-known open-source agentic systems, it found warped formatters in both. We opened PRs to fix both, and the OpenClaw fix has already been merged. Practitioners can run the same prompt on their own systems today.

2610.33465.title: LegoSR: A Unified Framework for Self-Improving Agent-Guided Scientific Discovery
2610.33465.authors: Hao Mao, Xu T. Liu, Hao Xu, Peng Zhao, Qian Li, Dongxiao Zhang, Jinyue Yan, Yuntian Chen
2610.33465.abstract: Discovering equations from data provides governing laws, constitutive relations and closure models for scientific understanding and prediction. Yet a method that succeeds on one system may fail on another or on noisy data, so discovery depends on expert trial and error. Unsuccessful searches can still reveal useful parts of an equation, but these clues must be recognized and combined. We present LegoSR, a unified framework for agent-guided equation discovery built on composable discovery and cumulative experience. Seven complementary equation discovery methods and shared computational modules form reusable building blocks, connected through a common equation representation. Researchers can launch discovery with one command and guide it with partially known equations. LegoSR Agent selects methods, revises searches using feedback and combines partial findings into new hypotheses. Its Experience Library consolidates graded outcomes into lessons that guide later tasks across equation families. Evaluation covers 134 algebraic regression problems, 40 ordinary differential equation targets and 25 partial differential equation problems at several noise levels, together with three case studies. On noisy PDEs, LegoSR Agent recovers more equations than seven expert-tuned methods combined and stays close to them on ODEs. It also exceeds a generic agent with the same model, tools and budget by up to 28 percentage points, with 63-73% shorter median wall-clock time on PDE problems.

2610.35031.title: PatentAgentBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents with Professional Patent Task Suites
2610.35031.authors: Yijie Hu, Wei Li, Junjie Zhou, Zhiqi Jiang, Yi Jin, Licong Xu, Xinkai Sun, Kai Duan, Lisha Zhang
2610.35031.abstract: Patent practice lies at the intersection of technical, legal, and linguistic work, making it challenging yet crucial to technological innovation. Recently, rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems have demonstrated the potential to complete realistic business workflows and even patent works. This raises a question: can current AI systems perform patent work reliably? Existing benchmarks cover a limited range of patent tasks and simplify evidence acquisition by providing reference materials or candidate documents. In this paper, we introduce PatentAgentBench, a benchmark comprising 510 instances across eight task suites: novelty search, freedom-to-operate (FTO) search, design FTO, invalidity search, claim charting, patent drafting, office-action response, and patent translation. Curated from real patent records and professional materials, the benchmark combines task-specific metrics with expert-reviewed annotations and rubrics. Retrieval tasks such novelty search, FTO, etc., require agents to search and compare patent collections without a supplied candidate pool. The drafting and OAR tasks assess the quality of agents' work given technical disclosure and office action notice. We evaluate seven LLMs across four agent harnesses on PatentAgentBench, finding that current systems still struggle to identify novelty, assess risk, and understand practitioner intent throughout patent workflows.

2610.40030.title: Cheap Retrieval and Observation Credit Assignment from One Quantity: The Value of Information
2610.40030.authors: Daniel Strauss, Nikolaos Sotirakis, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
2610.40030.abstract: Memory in reinforcement learning raises two problems. Attention finds the relevant item by scoring the whole store, which is costly for robots under latency and energy limits. When a retrieved memory pays off, credit for acquiring it must cross the whole sequence. We argue that both are governed by one quantity, the value of information, and propose to estimate it from archived rollouts. We show that, read at the observation, it yields a lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action. This bound floors the action's TD target and credits the observation that earned it. Read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. This work-in-progress submission does not yet test this algorithm. Still, a pilot retrieval system learns to approximate an optimization problem introduced by the proposed algorithm.

2610.41044.title: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
2610.41044.authors: Khawaja Abaid Ullah, Ananya Acharya, Mohammad Javad Khojasteh
2610.41044.abstract: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-based consensus team and independent agents under five network conditions. Breach rates were 15% for the consensus team, 32% for the commander and 29% for independent agents. Burst message loss, falsified reports and limited radio range raised the commander's breach rate by 10 to 18 percentage points (pp), whereas the consensus team's changed by at most 5. In the consensus team, giving a low-cost LLM more authority over the bid computation raised its breach rate by 38 pp. With birds and civilian drones in airspace, we added an image for each to the input text state. Only the near-frontier model treated them apart from intruders. Intruders disguised as existing taxidermy bird drones were mistaken for birds by both low-cost and near-frontier LLMs, being dropped from pursuit in 59-61% of near-frontier decisions (1-16% before). However, a one-sentence forewarning in the prompt lowered it to 0-25%. We find that the LLM team with a dedicated external conflict-resolution protocol had the fewest breaches. The code is available at https://github.com/the-kas-lab/consensus-within-competition-between.

2611.02414.title: SGR-OPSD: Learning from Subgoal Plans with Graph-Regularized Credit Assignment for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
2611.02414.authors: Shu Liu, Yang Chong, WenShi Chen, Man Lan
2611.02414.abstract: OPSD provides dense supervision for agentic reinforcement learning through privileged information feedback. However, existing privileged information often lacks explicit task-progression planning, while teacher-student log-probability gaps reflect shifts in model preference rather than true task progress. To address these limitations, we propose Subgoal-Guided Graph-Regularized OPSD (SGR-OPSD), a framework that combines subgoal supervision with interaction-derived evidence for turn-level credit assignment. Specifically, SGR-OPSD uses LLM-generated subgoal plans to provide dense action-level guidance, converting them into advantage weights via a constrained, KL-regularized objective. To ground credit in observed outcomes, we construct a Subgoal Progress Graph that estimates empirical returns from sampled transition frequencies. The graph compares empirical action returns against the state average to derive preferences that calibrate the teacher's credit weights. Evaluated on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA across two model scales (Qwen2.5-3B and 7B), SGR-OPSD consistently outperforms GRPO and strong self-distillation baselines, improving success rates over GRPO by up to 7.6 percentage points and reaching 85.8% on ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B. Ablation studies confirm that subgoal guidance and graph-based weight calibration are key to these performance gains.

2611.03100.title: LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning
2611.03100.authors: Anna Gogleva, Thomas Charman, Martin Balla, Karl Gemayel
2611.03100.abstract: [Note, November 2026: the experimental results in this version are affected by implementation issues in the simulation environment and should not be relied upon pending correction. See the author note on page 1.] An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately. Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code: https://github.com/RelationRx/luca.

2611.03330.title: The SIMPLE Law for Energy Cost of LLM Inference
2611.03330.authors: Hiari Pizzini Cavagna, Andrea Proia, Daniele Cesarini, Zeynep Kiziltan, Andrea Bartolini
2611.03330.abstract: Generative AI is billed per token, yet tokens are not equally expensive. Each token enters the KV-cache and raises the cost of those that follow, so energy grows non-linearly along a sequence whose tokens look identical. No analytical model states what a token costs without per-LLM fitting, and no law names the factors that set it. From closed-form expressions of LLM inference's computational and memory-access complexity, we derive the SIMPLE Inference Model to Predict LLMs Energy (SIMPLE), a four-parameter law that separates prefill from decode, and decode into KV-cache and next-token computation cost. Over traces of 13 dense LLMs from several families on NVIDIA H100 GPUs, it attains R2 = 0.969 and 11.97% MAPE, 3.1-3.5x below the SOTA, without per-LLM calibration. SIMPLE explains as well as predicts: prefill energy grows quadratically with hidden dimension, so larger LLMs suffer most from long inputs; and higher GQA KV grouping reduces the per-token energy linearly relative to standard MHA. Increasing the reasoning token budget pushes output length beyond the analytically derived energy minimum, driving super-linear energy growth; accuracy rises but energy rises faster, so Intelligence per Joule peaks at an intermediate budget and falls by up to 3.14x across a 4.0x range. Moving to agentic serving raises energy per request by 13.0x, as both prefill and KV-cache terms grow with input length; prefix caching removes most of the prefill cost (-93%), but not KV-cache cost, so even a cached agentic request costs 4.8x more.

2611.07920.title: How Finite Brains Generalize Without Bound: Spatial Memory as a Universal Computer
2611.07920.abstract: A child who learned to add small numbers adds numbers of any length. LSTMs and Transformers trained on short sequences fail on longer ones. We trace this to what learners read when deciding. A position, count or time takes new values as input grows: it is a coordinate, and a learner that reads one meets in every long input values its experience never covered. Whether two things are the same has the same two answers at every size: it is a coincidence, and a learner that reads only coincidences finds in a long input nothing that short inputs lacked, so finite experience fixes its rule for every size. The memory carries the size of the input and the rule stays finite, and this determines the memory a generalizing brain can have: a memory that grows while what the learner reads of it stays finite has to look the same from every place, so it is made of cycles, and the past is reached by asking what happened when the cycles last stood where they stand now. The cycles are the grid modules, the cells that detect their return the place cells, the records the hippocampal index; a prefrontal controller moves the cycles and never sees them. Reading only coincidences costs no power: what finite experience fixes in such a learner is what Turing machines compute in step with their input, which is why a circuit that evolved to find the way home can learn arithmetic and grammar. In a network of neurons this machine of cycles is the dynamics seen through its symmetry, and symbols are its invariants. Trained on strings up to 40 symbols, the machine solves five benchmark tasks that no LSTM or Transformer solves, among them duplication and binary addition, and beyond the reach of its cycles it fails on the curve the theory predicts. Given larger cycles after training, a machine that saw no string longer than five symbols reverses a string of a million without error. Its controllers run unchanged on neurons.

2611.08684.title: Cancellation Is Not Enough: What Retries Leave Behind in an Overloaded LLM Engine
2611.08684.abstract: Clients and proxies in front of an LLM engine retry calls that time out. After a transient overload, these retries can keep the engine from recovering even when calls arrive below its capacity. Since the engine may keep computing for clients that have left, propagating cancellation looks like the natural remedy. In this paper, we test it on vLLM with overload experiments on three open models, and with scheduler traces of one that follow each client attempt to the execution it creates in the engine. We find that with retries on, cancellation alone did not restore service in any run, and only 12-38% of the calls that arrived after the overload were delivered. The traces suggest why: retries that vLLM ran typically started prefill less than half a second before they timed out. Executions that vLLM later aborted took 79-85% of the prompt tokens it computed, and vLLM's prompt-token counter missed a third to half of all computed prompt tokens. A retry budget restored service by shedding retries but left many of the overload's calls undelivered. Request coalescing delivered every call from the overload onward, some late, unless cancellation had already aborted the running execution. Overload controls should thus be judged by the executions that retries add and the calls that clients receive.

2611.11368.title: BiVerify: Closing the Loop Between Backward and Forward Verification for Mathematical Self-Correction
2611.11368.authors: Rui Zou, Xin Zhao, Mengqi Wei, Ji-Rong Wen
2611.11368.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made substantial progress in mathematical reasoning but still produce incorrect solutions to complex problems, indicating the need for more reliable self-correction mechanisms. Mathematical self-correction typically identifies errors through verification, which can proceed backward or forward. The two directions provide complementary verification capabilities. Backward verification checks a candidate answer against the original constraints, bypassing complex intermediate reasoning, but cannot ensure correct reasoning or objective completeness. Forward verification follows the problem conditions and current solution, enabling it to locate reasoning errors and assess objective completeness, but may overlook key constraints in complex solution chains. We propose BiVerify, a dynamically scheduled framework for bidirectional mathematical verification. BiVerify begins with backward verification to screen the answer against the original constraints, followed by forward verification of the reasoning process; subsequent direction switching, state resetting, and re-verification are governed by verification outcomes. Upon failure, the system revises the candidate or verification flow until the same candidate passes both directions. We also introduce shared mathematical tools that separate logical reasoning from precise computation. We systematically evaluate BiVerify on five challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks using multiple mainstream DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini models. BiVerify exceeds the strongest representative public baseline evaluated in this work by 13.5 percentage points in average accuracy, with the margin reaching 31.2 percentage points on GPT. Further analysis shows that BiVerify's overall performance exceeds that of either verification direction alone.

2611.11995.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
2611.11995.authors: Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, Rulin Shao, Yuetai Li, Niqi Lyu, Yicheng Ding, Shu Yang, Zhichen Zeng, Banghua Zhu, Jiaxin Pei, Kaize Ding, Pradeep Dasigi, Dan Roth, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, Teng Xiao, Radha Poovendran
2611.11995.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon

2611.12200.title: Learning to Act with World Models by Valuing What Comes Next
2611.12200.authors: Chenghao Gao, Zhi Zhang, Dian Jin, Yihe Pan, Doudou Zhou
2611.12200.abstract: A sparse terminal reward tells an agent little about its steps. Much of the missing information is implicit in the environment's dynamics, because each state transition can change the conditions for success long before the reward arrives. A world model trained on real transitions can learn to predict what each action changes, but a predicted observation does not by itself show whether success has become more likely. With a binary terminal reward, PPO's critic makes this judgment by estimating the current policy's probability of success, but only for states the agent reaches. Our method, WM-PPO, elegantly brings the two together. For each action the policy samples, executed or not, the world model predicts the next observation and the critic values the predicted successor. In the policy channel, comparisons among these values give the policy auxiliary advantages; in the value channel, their mean gives the critic an auxiliary target. A shared gate weights both channels according to how reliably comparisons with similar margins predicted real outcomes earlier in training. The policy, critic and world model all learn from the agent's own interaction, with no teacher or privileged information, and only the policy is used at inference. With a comparable number of real environment steps, WM-PPO raises success from PPO's 63.5% to 87.5% on ALFWorld and from 39.3% to 52.9% on ScienceWorld. It matches the strongest PPO refinements we tested on ALFWorld and exceeds the best of them by 6.5 points on ScienceWorld. The trained policy more often completes prerequisite steps before placing an object or committing to an answer.

2611.12307.title: PACE-ECG: Patient-Aware Contrastive ECG Pretraining; Leveraging Longitudinal Structure for Transferable Representations
2611.12307.authors: Riccardo Cavarra, Lupo Lovatelli, Shaheim Ogbomo-Harmitt, Jakub Grzelak, Adelaide De Vecchi, Andrew King, Oleg Aslanidi
2611.12307.abstract: Foundation models for physiological signals are commonly evaluated on in-domain interpretation tasks, but their ability to transfer to longitudinal clinical prognosis across healthcare systems remains uncertain. We developed PACE-ECG, an ECG pretraining framework that combines contrastive learning across temporally neighbouring recordings from the same patient with clinically guided multitask supervision. We evaluated frozen ECG representations for post-myocardial-infarction all-cause mortality and incident heart failure prediction across MIMIC-IV and two external HEEDB cohorts, comparing the proposed representation with DeepECG-SSL, a state-of-the-art model, and two control baselines. Across both downstream tasks, the proposed model outperformed DeepECG-SSL in-domain (AUROC +1.9% for mortality and +4.0% for heart failure) and on external populations in HEEDB-Boston (+5.6% for mortality +10.3% for heart failure) and HEEDB-Atlanta (+6.9% for mortality +11.0% for heart failure) while using an encoder 41 times smaller and a fraction of the pretraining data. A matched ablation showed that patient-temporal pairing improved external mortality and heart failure AUROC over generic self-supervision by 7.0% and 9.4% on HEEDB-Boston and 8.9% and 9.3% on HEEDB-Atlanta. These findings indicate that pretraining-objective design greatly influences downstream transfer alongside model and data scale, and that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to establish the clinical generalisability of ECG foundation representations.

2611.12942.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
2611.12942.abstract: A churn model is useful through the customers it selects for a retention offer: the better model is the one whose selection makes the campaign more profitable. Tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained networks that predict from a table of labelled examples without being trained on it, were recently reported to decisively outperform tree ensembles for churn. That comparison, however, used untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and ranking metrics only. We ask whether the advantage holds against tuned GBDTs when models are judged by expected campaign profit and by the reliability of their probabilities. Four TFMs (TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast, TabICL v2) face LightGBM, XGBoost and CatBoost tuned with Optuna on validation AUC, on five public telecom datasets, three from real operators, with 10 repeated splits each and 20 pre-declared comparisons tested with a corrected t-test and Holm correction. TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more expected maximum profit (EMP) than each tuned GBDT on two datasets, Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%). On Orange it is ahead in every split (14.3%), but not significantly after correction, and no TFM differs significantly from the GBDTs on the two fictional datasets. Across 27 assumed combinations of customer value, incentive cost and acceptance rate, TabPFN-3.5 stays ahead on all three real-operator datasets, though the size of its gain varies widely. Retuning the GBDTs on EMP moved no gap by more than 0.014 per customer. Ranking and probability reliability diverge: raw TabICL v2 underpredicts churn on Orange, and a threshold policy built on its probabilities loses 15.7% of attainable profit until it is recalibrated. Because the splits resample the same customers, the results describe these datasets, not telecom operators in general. The non-commercial licence of the TabPFN weights, rather than scoring cost, restricts production use.

2611.12961.title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
2611.12961.authors: Shuaijun Chen, Omid Tavallaie, Xin Chen, Wentao Gao, Nguyen H. Tran, Albert Y. Zomaya
2611.12961.abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

2611.13015.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
2611.13015.authors: Yuhan Tang, Ke Fan, Xinkai Zou, Baichuan Mo, Kangxin Cui, Ao Qu, Ou Zheng, Jiangbo Yu, Xuan Jiang, Haris N. Koutsopoulos, Jinhua Zhao, Yuan Zhou
2611.13015.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.

2611.13030.title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
2611.13030.authors: Xiaoyang Xing, Chun-Mei Feng, Anthony Cohn, Xiaoliang Gong, Asoke Nandi
2611.13030.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $\pi_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

2611.14017.title: Personalized Memory Rubrics: Learning What to Remember per User via Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment
2611.14017.authors: Yupeng Han, Kai Zhang, Shuochen Liu, Ze Liu, Xianquan Wang, Zhihong Pan, Xiangyu Zhao, Qi Liu, Enhong Chen
2611.14017.abstract: Long-horizon personalized agents maintain an evolving memory by continuously deciding what to add, modify, or discard. However, learning an optimal update policy remains challenging. Conventional training relies solely on terminal question-answering accuracy, yielding a coarse feedback signal that treats all intermediate updates identically. Furthermore, update utility is inherently user-specific, as identical memory actions may yield opposite effects across different user personas. Existing methods fail to address this heterogeneity, relying on globally shared evaluation standards with at most a single scalar intermediate reward. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{Personalized Memory Rubrics} (\textbf{PMR}), a framework that translates terminal feedback into fine-grained, per-step, and per-user credit assignment. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a specialized delta over the universal baseline. Through \textbf{Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment}, PMR redistributes credit at the token level, selectively amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones to avoid unreliable attribution. The rubric and memory policy \textbf{co-evolve} in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees. Crucially, PMR incurs zero inference overhead, operating without any rubric or external judge during deployment. Extensive experiments across four benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.

2611.14804.title: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
2611.14804.authors: Noah J. Bagazinski, Cyril Picard, Faez Ahmed
2611.14804.abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

2611.14965.title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling
2611.14965.authors: Jie Ren, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Neil Thompson
2611.14965.abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.

2611.15225.title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark
2611.15225.authors: Shunming Liu, Jianyi Peng, Cheng Li, Lu Hou, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
2611.15225.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

2611.15592.title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
2611.15592.abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0-3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3-82.0% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1-2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.

2611.16493.title: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing
2611.16493.authors: Zipeng Ye, Shenyu Dai, Yong Xie, Kun Wang, Jiyang Guan, Zhikai Chen, Jiaqi Weng, Jialing Tao, Hui Xue
2611.16493.abstract: As agents perform tasks autonomously in local and cloud environments, auditing their execution trajectories can help service providers identify risks and improve agent harnesses and foundation models. Our analysis of production and red-team trajectories shows that some risks are repeatedly missed across auditing configurations. Overall recall obscures which risks are missed and whether higher recall comes with more false positives on legitimate behavior. Existing benchmarks offer limited insight into these failures. Generated trajectories can contain inconsistent tool calls and responses, conspicuous risky actions, or repetitive attack patterns. Grouping results by risk type also makes it difficult to tell whether auditors overlooked evidence, accepted an unsupported conclusion, or lacked information needed to make a judgment. We introduce ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for auditing responsible agent behavior. It organizes auditing challenges into six tiers: internal safety knowledge, contradictions within trajectories, evidence retrieval in long contexts, verification of sources and reasoning, indirect steering, and missing information. It includes challenging benign cases in which actions resemble risky ones but are consistent with the task and its authorization. It also provides paired trajectory versions to test whether auditors detect the same risks more reliably when the trajectory is shortened or missing information is supplied. Most samples are drawn from real production trajectories, with scenarios manually selected and adapted to preserve realistic tasks and risks that could plausibly arise during execution.

2611.16591.title: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
2611.16591.authors: Yang Zhou, Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Zerui Wang, Zhenyu Zhang, Wenshuang Li, Xinpeng Wei, Zhichen Zeng, Jingyu Liu, Jue Wang, Sen Wu, Ziheng Jiang, Zhen Dong, Han Cai, Binhang Yuan, Ying Sheng, Ce Zhang, Bo Li, Beidi Chen
2611.16591.abstract: Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.60. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.

2611.16647.title: InertiaMPDD: Multimodal Personalized Depression Detection via Emotional Inertia-Inspired Dynamics Modeling
2611.16647.authors: Changzeng Fu, Songyang Wang, Chang Gao, Xinyi Zhang, Peilin Li, Mo Meng, Jiarui Wu, Mingze Li, Hongwei Ding, Shiqi Zhao, Yong Li, Lang He
2611.16647.abstract: Multimodal depression screening estimates risk from speech, visual behavior and language. Current methods mainly predict labels, with limited evidence of departures from a non-depressed reference. Recording-level supervision also leaves fine-grained emotional dynamics unannotated. Motivated by emotional inertia, the persistence of affect, InertiaMPDD learns healthy next-state patterns using a world-model-inspired latent predictor. Using pretrained multimodal representations, it predicts from observed history and context. Reference deviation, residual decay rate and a Jacobian spectral descriptor form reference-derived emotional dynamics descriptors, evaluated as candidate proxy biomarkers for standalone screening and personalized decision correction. Across five cohorts from four datasets, fusion reaches 98.41% F1 on D-Vlog and 84.98% on LMVD. Standalone descriptors outperform fixed additive fusion on MPDD but discriminate weakly on AVEC2014. These findings distinguish reference informativeness from fusion benefit and reveal context-dependent utility.

2611.17007.title: Skill Adapter: Personalized Modification and Online Routing of General-Purpose Skills
2611.17007.authors: Qijia Zhuang, Yanyin Gou, Wenbin Ma, Yuxiang Ren
2611.17007.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents use external skills to reuse task procedures and experience with tools. General-purpose skills describe shared execution procedures, while specific tool choices, operating practices, and output requirements vary across users. In long-horizon tasks, subgoals, available inputs, and environmental states change as execution progresses. Agents must select currently applicable skills from an expanding skill pool and prepare candidates for subsequent steps. We propose Skill Adapter, which enables personalized modification and online routing of general-purpose skills. The system distills local adjustments from user requirements and execution feedback and stores them as Adapters linked to general-purpose skills. The routing agent selects general-purpose skills and applicable Adapters based on the current subtask, execution progress, and environmental feedback, incrementally maintaining a task-level online skill library that the main LLM reads on demand. The system preloads candidates for subsequent nodes and rechecks their applicability once actual inputs are determined. Reinforcement learning optimizes the two types of decisions using modification gains and routing outcomes, respectively. We evaluate Skill Adapter on ALFWorld, WebShop, and SkillsBench. Compared with SkillRL, it improves task success rates by an average of 11.43 percentage points and reduces mean execution time on all three benchmarks. Skill Adapter retains its performance advantage when the skill pool grows to 1,000 skills.

2611.17704.title: An AI-enabled high-resolution chlorophyll-a forecasting model that outperforms the operational global biogeochemical system
2611.17704.authors: Yong Jiang, Zheng Jiang, Gaowei Zhang, Zengzhou Hao, Suixiang Shi, Chi Zhang, Wei Wang
2611.17704.abstract: Surface chlorophyll-a concentration is a key indicator of marine phytoplankton variability, and short-term forecasts of its distribution provide advance information for marine ecosystem monitoring and management. However, interactions between physical transport and biological processes complicate chlorophyll-a forecasting, and simulating these coupled processes with conventional numerical models imposes substantial computational demands. Here we introduce ChlCast, an AI model that generates daily forecasts of surface chlorophyll-a concentration over a 10-day horizon at approximately 4-km resolution between 60$^\circ$S and 60$^\circ$N. ChlCast combines factorized spatiotemporal convolutions with a multiscale architecture to learn from historical chlorophyll-a fields and climatological information. Compared with the operational 0.25$^\circ$ Copernicus global ocean biogeochemical forecasting system, ChlCast reduces mean absolute error and root mean square error by 70.74% and 47.63%, respectively, against satellite-derived Level-4 chlorophyll-a fields, and by 35.03% and 13.07% against independent BGC-Argo in situ observations. Coastal case studies further show that the 4-km forecasts retain coastal gradients and localized concentration maxima that are weakened by coarse-grid averaging. These results demonstrate the potential of observation-driven deep learning for high-resolution forecasting of surface chlorophyll-a variability at the near-global scale.

2611.18464.title: Typing Matters: Muscle, Language and Typing Behaviour in Live Keystroke Decoding from sEMG
2611.18464.authors: Abhilash Durgam, Nyle Siddiqui, Mubarak Shah, Qiushi Fu
2611.18464.abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) from the wrists can recover typed text without a keyboard. It is usually posed as a signal-inference problem: characters are read out of the muscle signal and character error rate is reported offline. We argue that this framing removes most of the problem. The decoder is constrained simultaneously by the muscles, by the language being typed, and by typing behaviour such as typos, corrections, backspaces and line breaks, and a usable system must predict keys live while the hand keeps moving. Existing systems fall short on two counts: (1) they process sEMG in fixed windows and carry nothing from one window to the next, discarding context accumulated over a session, and (2) they lack any understanding of the linguistic structure that drives typing, so every keystroke is inferred from the muscle signal alone. We propose a fully causal, zero-lookahead sEMG typing decoder built on a state space model (SSM), in which a single model decodes a whole session without windowed partitions, conditioned on what has already been typed. We achieve this by fusing a traditional typing decoder with an efficient autoregressive language model, instilling both sEMG and linguistic understanding in one model. To train such a model for per-character typing rather than whole-word text, we introduce a retokenization method that rewrites ordinary prose as human-like typing, with keystrokes, typos, backspaces and line breaks included, converting WikiText into a large typing corpus where none existed. Our model, having never seen a single sEMG-to-character transcript in typing, achieves a state-of-the-art character error rate of 25.13% on emg2qwerty's cross-user benchmark, a 5.4% relative improvement over the previous best with 6.7 times fewer parameters, while running strictly causally with no future context.

2304.04308.title: Ensemble Modeling for Time Series Forecasting: an Adaptive Robust Optimization Approach
2304.04308.authors: L\'eonard Boussioux, Henry Mao, Dimitris Bertsimas
2304.04308.abstract: Accurate time-series forecasting is critical for many problems involving temporal data. Ensemble modeling is a well-established technique that leverages multiple predictive models to improve accuracy and robustness, since a single predictor's performance can vary widely due to shifts in the underlying data distribution. This paper proposes a new methodology for building robust ensembles of time series forecasting models. Our approach uses Adaptive Robust Optimization (ARO) to construct a linear regression ensemble whose model weights adapt over time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through synthetic experiments covering eight disturbance scenarios, from no drift to abrupt regime shifts, and real-world applications, including air pollution management, energy consumption forecasting, and tropical cyclone intensity forecasting. In the real-world applications, our adaptive ensembles outperform the best ensemble member in hindsight by 16-26% in root mean square error (RMSE) and 14-28% in conditional value at risk at the 15% level and improve over the other ensemble methods we compare on most metrics. In the synthetic experiments, they have lower mean RMSE than a rolling-ridge comparator in seven of the eight scenarios, significantly in four, while an abrupt regime shift that first appears after model selection remains a limitation.

2312.10181.title: Integrating Fairness and Model Pruning Through Bi-level Optimization
2312.10181.authors: Yucong Dai, Gen Li, Feng Luo, Xiaolong Ma, Yongkai Wu
2312.10181.abstract: Deep neural networks achieve high predictive performance but often require substantial computational and storage resources, which motivates model compression techniques such as neural network pruning. Conventional pruning methods, however, can introduce or amplify algorithmic bias and produce disparate outcomes across demographic groups. We study fair model pruning, which seeks sparse models that satisfy fairness criteria while maintaining predictive performance. We characterize fairness using both group accuracy disparity and differences in compression-induced accuracy degradation across demographic groups. We propose a framework that jointly optimizes pruning masks and model weights under fairness constraints, thereby integrating accuracy and fairness into the compression process. We formulate fair pruning as a constrained bi-level optimization problem and derive an efficient optimization procedure. Experiments across multiple datasets, predictive tasks, model architectures, and sparsity levels show that our framework improves the trade-off among fairness, accuracy, and training efficiency relative to the baseline pruning strategies. Compared with the strongest evaluated baselines, BiFP maintains competitive accuracy and fairness while requiring more than 94% fewer training iterations in the real-world experiments.

2406.05364.title: Could Mobile AI be Exploited?: Understanding the Exploitations of Trust and Ethics Gap in On-Device Small Language Models
2406.05364.authors: Kalyan Nakka, Jimmy Dani, Nitesh Saxena
2406.05364.abstract: In this paper, we present a very first study to investigate trust and ethical implications of on-device artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on small language models (SLMs) amenable for personal devices like smartphones. While on-device SLMs promise enhanced privacy, reduced latency, and improved user experience compared to cloud-based services, we posit that they might also introduce significant risks and vulnerabilities compared to their on-server counterparts. As part of our study, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the state-of-the-art on-devices SLMs, compared to their on-server counterparts, using well-established trust and ethics frameworks. Our results illustrate that on-device SLMs are significantly less trustworthy and lacks ethical safeguards, specifically demonstrating more stereotypical, unfair, privacy-breaching and harmful content generation behavior. Further, these risks of on-device SLMs could be exploited through Open Knowledge (OkNow) Attacks, and we demonstrated them using potentially unethical vanilla prompts, to which the on-device SLMs answer with valid responses without any filters and without the need for any jailbreaking or prompt engineering. These responses can be abused for various harmful and unethical scenarios like: societal harm, illegal activities, hate, self-harm, exploitable phishing content, disinformation and many others.

2410.07158.title: quanda: An Interpretability Toolkit for Training Data Attribution Evaluation
2410.07158.authors: Dilyara Bareeva, Galip \"Umit Yolcu, Anna Hedstr\"om, Niklas Schmolenski, Thomas Wiegand, Wojciech Samek, Sebastian Lapuschkin
2410.07158.abstract: Training data attribution (TDA) methods estimate the influence of individual training samples on a model's predictions, offering a principled lens for interpreting neural networks. Despite rapid methodological progress, TDA evaluation remains scattered across papers and rarely reproducible, making fair comparison between methods challenging. We introduce quanda, a Python toolkit that standardizes TDA evaluation. quanda features a comprehensive collection of evaluation metrics and ready-to-use benchmarks spanning image classification, text classification, and language modeling, alongside a uniform interface for integrating diverse TDA implementations. We showcase quanda through a comparative study of existing TDA methods and find that no approach excels uniformly across metrics, with clear trade-offs between ground-truth faithfulness and downstream task performance. By consolidating the tooling around TDA, quanda equips the community to evaluate attribution methods rigorously and reproducibly. The toolkit is thoroughly tested, documented, and available as an open-source library on PyPI and at https://github.com/dilyabareeva/quanda.

2501.13946.title: Hallucination Mitigation using Agentic AI Natural Language-Based Frameworks
2501.13946.abstract: Hallucinations remain a significant challenge for Generative AI, undermining trust in AI systems and their reliability. This study investigates how orchestrating multiple specialized AI agents can mitigate hallucinations, with a focus on systems that use Natural Language Processing (NLP) for agent interaction. We design a pipeline that feeds 310 prompts, purposefully crafted to induce hallucinations, into a front-end agent; its outputs are reviewed and refined by second- and third-level agents that detect unverified claims, add explicit disclaimers and clarify speculative content. We introduce four novel Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) - Factual Claim Density, Factual Grounding References, Fictional Disclaimer Frequency and Explicit Contextualization Score - aggregated into a Total Hallucination Score (THS) and assessed by a dedicated fourth-level evaluator agent. Inter-agent context is carried by the Open Floor Protocol (OFP, formerly OVON, Open Voice Network), whose structured JSON messages let each reviewer pass its assessment of hallucination likelihood, and the reasons behind it, to the next stage. Across the 310 prompts, THS improves by a mean of -0.131 per prompt from the front-end agent to the final reviewer (Cohen's d = 2.38), with lower scores on 302 of 310 prompts. The gain is carried mainly by explicit disclaimers and contextualization, making speculative content more transparent and clearly demarcated from factual claims. The results show that multi-agent orchestration with structured, NLP-based exchange of meta-information can substantially strengthen the epistemic framing of AI-generated responses and improve their explainability.

2503.08823.title: ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
2503.08823.abstract: Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

2504.02293.title: Breaking the Silence: A Dataset and Benchmark for Bangla Text-to-Gloss Translation
2504.02293.authors: Sharif Mohammad Abdullah, Abhijit Paul, Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Zarif Masud, Shebuti Rayana, Ahmedul Kabir
2504.02293.abstract: Gloss is a written approximation that bridges Sign Language (SL) and its corresponding spoken language. Despite a deaf and hard-of-hearing population of at least 3 million in Bangladesh, Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) remains largely understudied, with very limited prior work on Bangla text-to-gloss translation and no publicly available parallel dataset at the time of this work. To address this gap, we construct the first publicly available Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, consisting of 1,000 manually annotated and 4,000 synthetically generated Bangla sentence-gloss pairs, along with 159 expert human-annotated pairs used as a test set. Our experimental framework performs a comparative analysis between several fine-tuned open-source models and a leading closed-source LLM to evaluate their performance in low-resource BdSL translation.
