The first limitation was recently addressed by the Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Business Cycle (MARL-BC), which places deep RL households in a real business cycle economy and reduces to classic DSGE models in specific limits. Here we address the second limitation. We present JaxMARL-BC, a JAX-accelerated simulator that trains MARL-BC economies in seconds (between 75x and 724x faster than the reference implementation), and scales to 200,000 independent learning households. We verify its correctness against the known DSGE limits, characterise its scaling through a simple cost law, and demonstrate its value by a proof-of-concept calibration of an extended model with heterogeneous returns on capital, in a two-hour experiment that would previously have taken over a month. We release JaxMARL-BC as open source.

2610.33012.title: Recursive Semantic Divergence for LLM Agent Consistency
2610.33012.authors: Harshavardhan Abichandani, Penny Chong, Atin Ghosh, Daniel Dahlmeier
2610.33012.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents with tool use can behave inconsistently across independent runs from identical states. They may call different tools, produce contradictory outputs, or follow divergent strategies. This variability compounds over time and undermines deployment reliability. Existing evaluation metrics primarily measure task correctness via completion-based scores and do not capture consistency in agent behavior across executions. Separately, agent behavior is analyzed either at the token level using probability distributions or at the single-response level using semantic clustering, but neither captures how inconsistency propagates across future turns of a trajectory. We introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level consistency metric adapted from bisimulation metrics in reinforcement learning. RSD measures the expected cumulative semantic disagreement between two independent rollouts of the same agent from the same state, using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistency. It is defined recursively over future states and approximated by a neural network trained on independent rollouts. The learned metric estimates future divergence from the current state, providing a consistency score at each turn without requiring the full trajectory to complete. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces AUC coefficient of variation (CV) by up to 30.9% on tau2-bench and 50.5% on ToolSandbox. Across Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5 models, RSD reduces AUC CV in seven out of eight model-benchmark settings, while improving the final task progress in all eight settings.

2610.37386.title: Channel Selection for Mixture-of-Experts Decoding Needs No Calibration Data
2610.37386.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are bottlenecked by loading routed-expert weights from memory during interactive decoding at small batch sizes. Because most intermediate channels in a routed expert contribute little to any single token, channel selectors predict which channels matter and read only their weights, typically keeping channels above a threshold calibrated on offline data. We show that channel selection needs no calibration data. First, a calibrated threshold does not fix how much a selector reads, because the number of channels passing it varies across inputs; Prox with thresholds calibrated for an 18% read budget actually reads only 12.9% on average across our benchmarks. Second, top-k keeps each token's k highest-scoring channels and needs no calibration data. At the calibrated budget, a selector's top-k version matches or beats its threshold version on the same score in 40 of 43 comparisons at 13% and 18% budgets, including all 23 on generation tasks. The top-k versions also avoid the repetition-loop collapse that calibrated thresholds cause on Gemma 4. Calibrating a threshold thus provides neither of the two things selectors use it for: a known read budget and a consistent accuracy gain at that budget. We furthermore introduce a reader built entirely from the model's weights, which screens channels with a ternary sketch and recovers the skipped ones with a low-rank map. Across three post-trained MoE models, our reader retains 98.1% of full-model accuracy at 17.8% of routed-expert reads, with Triton kernels running MoE blocks 1.60 to 1.90x faster than optimized vLLM at batch one and up to 2.69x at larger batches on the same three models.

2610.37584.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
2610.37584.authors: Yuxi Huang, Silin Zhou, Chenhao Wang, Zihan Li, Gangming Guo, Pei Ke, Shen Gao, Shuo Shang
2610.37584.abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We formalize item-level preference distillation on the SID prefix tree, deriving an exact factorization of item preference distributions into prefix conditionals and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into conditional KL terms. Guided by this decomposition, we renormalize the generator's probabilities over legal next tokens and match the resulting distributions to the teacher's conditional preferences along the ground-truth SID path, jointly optimizing the distillation objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation and demonstrate that REGER consistently outperforms existing GR baselines while retaining efficient inference.

2610.38214.title: Skeleton Coding: Program Structure as Control for AI Agents
2610.38214.authors: Aditya Golatkar, Alessandro Achille, Renos Zabounidis, Vlad Sobal, Yangruibo Ding, Baishakhi Ray, Jonathan Buck, Guy Van den Broeck, Maryam Fazel, Pietro Perona, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
2610.38214.abstract: Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input-output examples. How many such specifications must users provide, and which ones, for the agent to implement a program that fulfills their intent? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, because it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure - that is, a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions - which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, users cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering such structure from thousands of lines of generated code. To address this issue, we introduce Skeleton Coding, a process in which humans jointly specify the structure in high-level, code-like format, alongside behavioral specifications for the desired outcome. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests users must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15-26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

2610.41291.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
2610.41291.authors: Xuning He, Kai Fan, Runyu Zhang, Binghuan Wang, Yuxiang Zhang, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong
2610.41291.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 59.84% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 12.3 to 194.9 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.

2610.41398.title: Distilling Knowledge from Search: Decoder Model Factory for Quantum LDPC Codes
2610.41398.authors: Anil Bilgin, Wanda Hou, Pranav Srinivas Murali, Yi-Zhuang You
2610.41398.abstract: We introduce GraphMP, a learning-based message-passing decoder for quantum low-density parity-check codes that transfers without fine-tuning across code families, code sizes, physical error rates, and noise models. Its local message passing keeps computation scalable as the decoding graph grows. We further embed GraphMP in a beam-search algorithm that progressively refines candidate error patterns, trading additional decoding time for lower logical error rates. To turn this decoding effort into lasting improvements, we propose the decoder model factory, a paradigm for training successive models on data collected by earlier models during decoding. In our implementation, verified search trajectories provide reusable training data for distilling knowledge into subsequent models. Across generations, the model factory yields a search-enhanced decoder that is broadly competitive with Relay-BP. On the largest code block, which encodes $4612$ logical qubits, it achieves a lower logical error rate and about $20$ times the decoding throughput of the standard Relay-BP baseline. These results motivate a coupled quantum-classical architecture with two interacting cycles: rapid decoding protects quantum information, while slower learning adapts the models to changing noise conditions. The long-term vision is a scalable decoder model factory that continually produces high-performance, low-latency decoders for evolving quantum hardware.

2611.00606.title: Sparse Autoencoder Attribution Graphs Are Decided at the Margin
2611.00606.abstract: Attribution graphs predict sparse autoencoder (SAE) ablations to first order on the active features, but a TopK SAE passes only its k largest preactivations, so small changes often swap active features. On five public TopK SAEs, zeroing one feature changes the active set of the next layer's SAE in 74% to 89% of cases. Our margin graph adds the first order change to every downstream preactivation, then selects the k largest again. On Pythia-70M the margin graph cuts the median error of predicted activations, relative to their exact change, from the attribution graph's 0.739 to 0.121, 84% lower. Exact recomputation of 48 interventions runs 3.5 times faster than the margin graph on our GPU. Patched into Pythia-70M with the clean reconstruction error, the margin graph's activations predict the change in the subject verb agreement logit difference with 1.95 times the attribution graph's mean error, on interventions above a fixed floor. Between seeds of our SAEs, which share one auxiliary loss coefficient, sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but 47% with each graph masked to its own, 38 percentage points less. Unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovers 73% of the masking loss, against 11% for a random tenth, so the margin to that threshold decides how ablations change activations and what graphs carry between seeds.

2611.00911.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
2611.00911.abstract: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.

2611.01631.title: Zero-shot evaluation of open vision-language models as System 1 decision models on radiology tasks
2611.01631.abstract: Purpose: To compare two multimodal System 1 decision models (Clef 27B, d1 3B) with three generative vision-language models read out zero-shot from a single answer token (Qwen3.8-27B, which is Clef's backbone; Gemma 4 31B; MedGemma 1.5 4B) on seven radiology tasks. Methods: All models ran locally on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The System 1 models returned a probability for each option in one pass; for the generative models, probabilities were read from the log-probabilities of the option letters. Tasks covered chest CT and radiograph reports (CT-RATE, PadChest), device MR safety records (GUDID), tubes and lines on chest radiographs (RANZCR CLiP), chest CT volumes (CT-RATE), brain MRI motion (MR-ART) and MRI sequence (BraTS 2021), 4,435 cases in total. The primary endpoint was AUROC with bootstrap 95% CIs. Results: All five models retrieved report findings well (AUROC 0.93-0.99). Clef ranked higher than its backbone on CT volumes (0.749 vs 0.668) and tube and line radiographs (0.812 vs 0.766) and lower on motion (0.625 vs 0.709), but it changed decisions more than ranking: it identified 90 of 100 FLAIR volumes, a class its backbone never chose, and cut calibration error on CT volumes from 0.436 to 0.072. d1 was within 0.04 of Clef on reports while using 3 to 9 times less energy per request, but was weak on images. Gemma 4 31B ranked device MR safety best (0.854) and MedGemma 1.5 4B ranked motion best (0.821), yet MedGemma was at chance on MRI sequences and answered "severe" for 93% of motion scans. Conclusion: A single-token readout turns open generative models from several families into usable decision models without retraining, but no model was best on every task and each had task-specific answer biases, so models and decision thresholds should be chosen on local cases.

2611.02688.title: Accelerating LLM Pretraining with Zeroth-Order Curvature on Idle Serving Compute
2611.02688.authors: Mingchuan Ma, Dongqi Cai, Daqian Yang, Zhenyan Lu, Chen Chen, Teresa Lv, Yan Gao, Shangguang Wang, Mengwei Xu, Nicholas D. Lane, Yu Huang
2611.02688.abstract: LLM pretraining is increasingly compute-intensive, while substantial inference serving compute remains idle during off-peak periods. However, such serving hardware is difficult to use for conventional first-order training due to its memory, networking and other system requirements. Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization offers a natural interface to this forward-only compute resource, but its gradient estimates break down in pretraining. Unlike fine-tuning, which can confine updates to a small parameter subspace, pretraining must update every parameter, and the alignment of a ZO gradient estimate with the true gradient shrinks as the number of updated parameters grows. We make a different observation: noisy ZO estimates can still provide useful curvature information, even when they are too inaccurate to serve as gradients. Based on this insight, we propose ZO-Curv, which leverages idle forward-only devices to estimate curvature and uses it to adapt and refine the update used during first-order training, thereby accelerating the process. We provide convergence guarantees that characterize the effect of finite-query curvature estimation. Experiments on LLMs from 125M to 1.5B parameters show that ZO-Curv consistently accelerates pretraining. At 770M parameters, ZO-Curv reaches AdamW's 20K-step validation loss in 3.9 hours instead of 7.5 hours, while achieving a lower final loss of 2.70 versus 2.84 under the same step budget. These results show that idle model serving compute can accelerate LLM pretraining when zeroth-order queries are used to estimate curvature rather than gradients directly.

2611.02721.title: IssueLighter: An Issue Type-Aware LLM Agent for Issue Report Validity Assessment
2611.02721.authors: Jiawei Ran, Yuxia Zhang, Ziyang Zhao, Hui Liu
2611.02721.abstract: Invalid issue reports are prevalent in open source software (OSS) projects, imposing substantial burdens on maintainers who already face a high risk of burnout. Prior research has primarily focused on identifying invalid reports for specific issue categories (e.g., bug and wontfix), leaving the broader landscape of OSS issue types largely unexplored and limiting the generalizability of existing approaches. Moreover, existing methods provide little support for explaining or validating their predictions, reducing their practical usefulness for maintainers. With the rise of LLM-based agents, it remains unclear whether a comprehensive understanding of the causes of invalidity across all issue types can improve validity assessment performance while producing well-grounded rationales. To this end, we first manually annotated the validity status of 520 issue reports from three OSS projects, i.e., pandas, scikit-learn, and mypy, resulting in 257 invalid reports and 263 valid ones. Then, we conducted a thematic analysis on these invalid reports and identified 13 causes of invalidity that are closely specific to issue types. Based on these insights, we propose IssueLighter, an agent-based framework with a type-aware validity assessment strategy that dynamically executes commands. Experimental results show that IssueLighter consistently and substantially outperforms all baseline methods, with an average F1 improvement of over 20 percentage points. Ablation studies confirm that both the type-aware strategy and the taxonomy of causes of invalidity contribute to the performance gains. Qualitative analysis further demonstrates that IssueLighter generates rationales grounded in accurately identified causes of invalidity and supported by evidence. Moreover, leveraging these rationales, we challenged maintainers' original decisions in four disputed cases, and all received approval.

2611.05726.title: Do Language Models Know Which Constraints Belong Together?
2611.05726.authors: Junbo Jacob Lian, Kaixuan Chen, Hanzhang Qin, Huiling Chen, Chaoyu Zhang, Chung-Piaw Teo
2611.05726.abstract: Dantzig--Wolfe reformulation strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, and each candidate costs a column generation run. The choice is hard when families strengthen the bound only together, as in classical lot-sizing, network-design, and facility-location formulations. We prove that when an evaluation convexifies at most $s$ of $k$ families, methods that observe only bounds need of order $k^w$ evaluations to find a hidden group of $w$ families in the worst case. A prediction missing $e$ members reduces this to $\Theta(k^e)$ through a staged search that need not know $e$. The orders extend to several groups, prices, and growing evaluation costs. We study two predictors: a lookahead at an optimal LP dual, which vanishes on groups whose families share no variable, and language models reading the model, verified by the staged search in JointDW. Such groups appear in three of ten MIPLIB-NL models whose bound can be improved and in all 59 benchmark instances. Given the coefficients of constructed models with up to 16 families, one language model names a true group first in 249 of 252 answers. On the benchmark instances, decompositions chosen by language models from the text solve faster than those of GCG's detector.

2611.07222.title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection
2611.07222.authors: Woosang Lim (SAINT Machines, KAIST), Yeseul Chang (Chung-Ang University), Jaewoo Lee (Chung-Ang University)
2611.07222.abstract: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .005. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

2611.07604.title: FisherDistill: Diffusion Distribution Distillation via Closed-Form Fisher Critics
2611.07604.authors: Mahesh Bhosale, Yuanhao Zhai, Siwei Lyu, Junsong Yuan, David Doermann, Defang Chen
2611.07604.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion distillation have enabled high-quality image generation in only one or a few network function evaluations (NFEs). Despite their efficiency, aggressively distilled generators often retain a residual distribution gap from their multi-step teachers, motivating recent methods to introduce adversarial refinement with a learned discriminator. In this work, we ask whether such refinement necessarily requires a learned adversarial discriminator. We introduce \textbf{FisherDistill}, a simple alternative based on Fisher linear discriminant analysis. Using intermediate representations from the frozen teacher, we estimate the first- and second-order statistics of real and generated samples and derive a closed-form Fisher direction that maximally separates their feature distributions relative to within-class variation. This direction provides a lightweight refinement signal that complements the original distillation objective without requiring an additional adversarial discriminator or its optimization loop. Across multiple distillation frameworks, our approach consistently improves generation quality over their respective distilled baselines and substantially closes the gap to adversarially refined counterparts. Code: https://bhosalems.github.io/FisherDistill/

2611.07940.title: CardioLM: A multilingual suite of small language models for the cardiology domain
2611.07940.authors: Manuela-Daniela Danu, Miguel Rodr\'iguez-Ortega, Alberto Becerra-Tome, Pablo Arancibia, Fernando Gallego-Donoso, Lorenzo Pratesi, Xi Bai, Andrei-Damian Dinescu, Salvador Lima-L\'opez, Andrea Guala, Saskia Haitjema, Jonas Mack, Michele Miranda, Wesam Al Nabki, Jan Rodr\'iguez-Miret, Vasile George Marica, Vladim\'ir Kincl, Kate\v{r}ina Dost\'alov\'a, Michael Andrej, Alicia Ujil, Corinne Allaart, Machteld Boonstra, Malin Overmars, Anoop Shah, Giovanna Ceroni, Jonathan Kossoff, Domenico D'Amario, Renzo Laborante, Antonio Iaconelli, Isabella Fumarulo, Jacopo Lenkowicz, Livia Lilli, Emma Weiss, Alex Scafa, Felix Lindberg, Milou Gamage, Eul\`alia Farr\'e-Maduell, S\'ebastien Brati\`eres, Martin Krallinger, Bram van Es
2611.07940.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular care generates large volumes of clinical free-text documentation in local languages. However, clinical natural language processing (NLP) resources remain concentrated in English, and no existing benchmark is cardiology-specific, multilingual, and broad in entity coverage. Methods: We present two contributions. The first is CardioCCC, a corpus of 508 cardiology case reports originally published in Spanish and extended to Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, and Swedish through machine translation, annotation projection, and clinician review, with annotations covering diseases, symptoms, procedures, and medications. The second is CardioLM, comprising CardioBERTa, a set of language-specific encoders obtained by continued pretraining on cardiology and biomedical corpora, and CardioNER, a set of named entity recognition (NER) models fine-tuned on CardioCCC. Results: Cardiology-specific pretraining reduced pseudo-perplexity by up to a factor of eight, yet changed strict span-level F1 by at most 0.04, with benefits concentrated in languages whose backbones lacked biomedical coverage. The jointly trained multilingual XLM-RoBERTa-large models achieved the best strict F1 in nearly every language and entity type, exceeding the strongest monolingual system by up to 0.13 F1. A large share of residual errors concerned boundary detection: relaxed matching recovered 0.10-0.23 F1 for disease, procedure, and symptom, but only 0.01-0.07 for medication. Clinicians rated CardioNER well above a rule- and dictionary-based baseline, with the mean rating across entity types rising from 26% to 73%. Conclusions: Specialty-specific pretraining is not the decisive factor for downstream entity recognition, whereas multilingual joint training yields the strongest results in nearly all settings and a simpler deployment path for multi-country clinical information extraction.

2611.08439.title: Label-Wording Augmentation in a Typed-Decision Encoder: Gains on Unfamiliar Words, Not on Abbreviations or Codes
2611.08439.abstract: Typed-decision models score options that the caller supplies at request time, so their accuracy depends on label wording that the model's developer does not control. We compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder, Ru-Jev, trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks; the later release adds an augmentation that presents labels in several surface forms. Holding questions fixed and varying only how eighteen routing labels are worded, we evaluate ten label vocabularies at five and eighteen candidates, checked for overlap with the training data. On held-out vocabularies made of ordinary or borrowed words (jargon, office slang, department names), the augmented release has higher point accuracy in all fourteen cells, by up to 0.24. Several of these gains rest partly on one label that the earlier release almost never chose; fitting one bias per option removes part of them, while the jargon gain largely survives. On abbreviations and opaque codes the augmented release gives no usable gain: its loss on 17 abbreviations unrelated to training (-0.060) is one label and disappears after the same correction. The comparison is between two trained releases, not a controlled ablation, and the earlier recipe varies across seeds by up to 0.098 on the strictest slice. On two datasets neither release saw, accuracy moves by -8.4 and +5.6 points, narrowed to -3.4 and +1.4 by the per-option biases; a second training run of each recipe, the augmented one under a rule recorded beforehand, puts the recipe gap on jargon far above seed noise and on a third unseen dataset, scientific rubrics, only just above it. Rankings of training checkpoints disagree across the three unseen datasets, so none of them should choose the checkpoint. We also report four evaluation hazards from comparing the two releases.

2611.09140.title: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music
2611.09140.authors: Phillip Long, Eduardo Escoto, Julian McAuley, Zachary Novack
2611.09140.abstract: Large public datasets have driven recent progress in machine learning, from text and vision to speech and general audio. Music remains an outlier, as copyright blocks redistribution of training audio, in particular for modern tasks that need individual stems rather than mixtures. Existing multitrack resources trade off realism, scale, and licensing, as synthetic alternatives rely on proprietary VSTs or naive open rendering that yields weak stems. We introduce SPDMX, an openly-licensed stem corpus rendered from the public-domain PDMX dataset. SPDMX comprises $5{,}469$ song-hours ($2{,}734$ song-hours, or $34.8\%$, of which are multitrack scores) at $44.1$ kHz under CC BY 4.0, with paired MIDI and identifiers that link our dataset to PDMX's original metadata. To our knowledge, SPDMX's multitrack subset constitutes the largest openly-licensed synthetic multitrack subset by song-hours. We then demo SPDMX as a dataset for both source separation and transcription, showing how its increased scale can enable better training of models on synthetic data. We release SPDMX, as well as the open creation pipeline for reuse on other symbolic music datasets.

2611.09218.title: BOXBOX: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Long-Running Performance Optimization
2611.09218.authors: Yuhao Tan, Hanyun Jiang, Fangkai Yang, Yuan Yao, Taolue Chen, Bo Qiao, Yu Kang, Lu Wang, Pu Zhao, Xiaoxing Ma, Qingwei Lin, Saravan Rajmohan, Qi Zhang
2611.09218.abstract: Automated harness optimization improves agents by learning from trajectories and task feedback. Existing offline methods use reference answers to optimize harnesses for reuse on held-out tasks. However, many real-world tasks are open-ended, while long runs expose new difficulties that offline-optimized harnesses may not address. To study harness optimization in these settings, we introduce PerfRace, a benchmark for long-running performance optimization of software projects, and investigate whether agents can use task-specific experience to recursively improve their harnesses during an ongoing task. To this end, we introduce BOXBOX, which enables agent-triggered harness revision and kernel-managed hot reloading while preserving execution context. We evaluate BOXBOX on PerfRace under matched test-time budgets, comparing it with Frozen Harness, offline Harness Evolution, and Harness Scaling. BOXBOX achieves higher speedup with more efficient use of task time and model cost, reaching a Speedup@4h of 1.70x, compared with 1.54x for the strongest baseline.

2611.09822.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
2611.09822.authors: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch, Eric Wieser, Francisco J. H. Heras, Nicholas C. Rubin, Guang Hao Low, S\'ebastien Racani\`ere, Nenad Toma\v{s}ev, Lei M. Zhang, James D. Watson, Tanuj Khattar, Aws Albarghouthi, Stavan Jain, Harun Khan, Leopoldo Sarra, Andrew W. Senior, Michael Broughton, Hussain Masoom, Sergio Boixo, Ryan Babbush, Swarat Chaudhuri, Pushmeet Kohli
2611.09822.abstract: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.57x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 12x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

2611.11172.title: Do Benign-Trained Hidden-State Probes Detect Tool Errors Under Adversarial Conditions?
2611.11172.abstract: Repeatedly training language models on their own generated data may create a synthetic-data feedback loop in which errors and distributional biases are reintroduced into subsequent training datasets. This paper studies that process in biomedical question answering (QA) using PubMedQA and two Qwen2.5 model sizes, 0.5B and 3B parameters. The study compares a recursive synthetic-data condition, in which generation G(k+1) is trained on answers produced by G(k), against a Human-Control condition that repeatedly uses the original human training data. The study evaluates across four generations from G0-G3 with two random seeds (42 and 123) and a fixed evaluation set of 1,000 expert-labeled samples. The evaluation includes disease and chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, lexical and semantic similarity, answer length, repetition rate, and other evaluation metrics. The Recursive condition for both model sizes and both seeds showed larger declines than the Human-Control condition in disease entity F1, chemical entity F1, context-supported rate, ROUGE-L, and cosine similarity. Under the fixed no-repeat 3-gram decoding constraint, the main observed behavioral change was increased answer length, while the measured 3-gram repetition rate did not increase. The magnitude of the difference-in-change was larger for the 3B model than for the 0.5B model. This difference was particularly apparent in disease F1, context-supported rate, cosine similarity, and answer length. These results show domain-specific changes associated with using recursive synthetic-data training in biomedical QA, but do not establish clinical hallucination rates or universal model collapse.

2611.12508.title: MARS: Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams for Video Forgery Detection
2611.12508.abstract: Generalizing deepfake detection across facial manipulation and fully generated video remains challenging due to forgery traces varying with the manipulation method and scene content. Explicit spatial and temporal feature differences offer a way to capture this variation, but also respond to natural texture and motion, motivating their joint interpretation with appearance features. We investigate whether combining multiscale feature differences with adapted appearance representations improves detection across both forgery categories. We introduce Multiscale Appearance-Residual Streams (MARS), a two-path video detector. The residual path applies fixed spatial and temporal difference-of-Gaussians operators to frozen intermediate features and models the resulting differences alongside appearance context across frames. The semantic path adapts the encoder's normalization parameters for frame classification, and a clip-dependent gate combines their predictions. Under a shared protocol across seven datasets, MARS achieves the highest average AUROC of 91.43\%, outperforming seven compared detectors. When trained on facial manipulations alone, MARS achieves 93.99\% AUROC on GenVideo and 75.50\% on DF26, demonstrating transfer to generated videos without generated-video training data. MARS also provides signed patch and frame contributions, whose faithfulness we evaluate through controlled spatial and temporal removal against random controls. MARS is publicly available for research: Project page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mars/ Github: https://github.com/VectorInstitute/mars

2611.12529.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
2611.12529.authors: Jingyi Zhang, Ruijun Sun, Klara Brandstatter, Nels Numan, Anthony Steed
2611.12529.abstract: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

2611.13058.title: The Indic Token Tax in 2026: Measuring Tokenizer. Disparity and Its Cost for the Languages of India
2611.13058.authors: Johin Johny Arimbur, Ankur Ashit Ghosh, Shervin Sam
2611.13058.abstract: Commercial language model APIs bill per token, so a tokenizer that needs more tokens for the same content in one language makes that language more expensive, slower, and able to fit less text in a fixed context window. We measure this disparity for nine public tokenizers, including those of GPT-4, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-V3, Mistral-Nemo and four Sarvam models, on all 25 languages of India available in FLORES-200 (2,009 professionally translated sentences aligned with English) and on 13,732 human-translated Hinglish-English social media pairs from PHINC. On GPT-4o's tokenizer the same content needs between 1.57 times (Hindi) and 5.01 times (Odia) the tokens of English, and 13.7 times for Santali in Ol Chiki script; GPT-4's tokenizer needs up to 12.8 times. Sarvam-30B/105B is the only third-party tokenizer that stays below 2.6 times on every language (median 1.53). In an illustrative scenario using official list prices accessed on 5 November 2026 and stated assumptions, a support bot handling 100,000 chats a month on GPT-4o would cost about INR 56,640 in English and INR 102,829 in Marathi; these are estimates, not measured production costs. Against an openly licensed Hindi and Marathi morphological segmentation set, no tokenizer places more than 35% of its word-internal boundaries on morpheme boundaries (boundary F1 at most 0.48). In a companion paper we present a tokenizer that reduces this tax. Code, pinned artifacts and raw token counts are available at https://github.com/HavonAI/indic-token-tax.

2611.13059.title: A Multi-Word Tokenizer for 204 Languages That Needs Fewer Tokens Than GPT-4o's, Including on English
2611.13059.authors: Johin Johny Arimbur, Ankur Ashit Ghosh, Shervin Sam
2611.13059.abstract: Languages of India need 1.6 to 14 times as many tokens as English on GPT-4o's tokenizer for the same content, which makes them more expensive and slower to serve. We train tokenizers from scratch on human-written text in about 200 languages. Havon v3 is a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 262,144 tokens and a pre-tokenizer that keeps combining marks with their letters and chunks scripts written without spaces. On FLORES-200 devtest it needs fewer tokens than GPT-4o's o200k_base on all 25 languages of India (median 0.74 of GPT-4o's count) and on 172 of 204 languages, but 7% more on English. Havon v4 adds a second, multi-word training stage (SuperBPE) to v3. At exactly GPT-4o's vocabulary size of 200,019 tokens, v4 needs 6.1% fewer tokens than GPT-4o on English and fewer on 161 of 204 languages and all 25 languages of India (median 0.74); at the same size, v3 needs 9.4% more on English and wins on 133. With 262,144 tokens, v4 needs 9.6% fewer tokens on English and fewer on 182 of 204 languages, and with 524,288 tokens it needs fewer on 203 of 204. The gains are largest for English, Hindi and the Romance languages; scripts without spaces, such as Khmer, Burmese and Tibetan, gain little and lose subword merges. Havon v5 replaces v4's Python-only code sample with permissively licensed code in 15 languages: on code it needs 1.03 to 1.22 times GPT-4o's tokens, against 1.11 to 1.29 for v4, while keeping all 25 languages of India (median 0.74, all significant under a sentence-level bootstrap) and English (0.94). These are compression results only: we have not yet evaluated a model trained with v4 or v5.

2611.14106.title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
2611.14106.authors: Martim Afonso, In\^es Lynce, Maurizio Morisio, Jo\~ao F. Ferreira
2611.14106.abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

2611.15108.title: Typed Knowledge over Constructive Institutions: A Proof-Relevant Type Theory for Verified Science
2611.15108.abstract: Mathematical proof assistants such as Coq, Agda, and Lean 4 build proof irrelevance into definitional conversion ($p \equiv q$ for $p, q : P$ with $P : Prop$), erasing which derivation established a theorem. While natural for mathematics over fixed axioms, judgmental proof irrelevance is incompatible with verified scientific stores, which must inspect and compare independent derivations of a claim to assess consilience and compute counterfactual retractions when an assay, reagent, or model is invalidated. Moreover, combining definitional proof irrelevance with subsingleton elimination breaks normalization and makes algorithmic conversion non-transitive. We present the type-theoretic and institutional foundations of Eigenius, a verified knowledge substrate for science. First, we formulate a dependent kernel with cumulative universes ($Prop, Set, Type_k$), impredicative $Prop$, inductive families with index-forced subsingleton elimination, and intensional identity types, where definitional equality $\equiv$ is untyped joinability under an orthogonal CRS and proof irrelevance is a witnessed axiom ($irrel : \Pi P{:}Prop.\,\Pi p,q{:}P.\,Id\,P\,p\,q$). Second, we unify universe cumulativity, $\Pi$-covariant subtyping, and ontology class inclusions in a coercion-free subsumption judgment whose bidirectional fragments ($\mathcal{K}_0, \mathcal{K}_1$) satisfy subject reduction, compile to unification-free checkers ($\mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1$), and match declarative typing. Third, we organize external verifiers into a three-level institutional hierarchy with explicit axiom policies (Adopt, Discharge, Relativize), internalize a justification logic with Why-provenance support $supp(j,P)$, and embed Cooper's Type Theory with Records (TTR) for open-world knowledge graphs. Finally, we prove consistency in Grothendieck universes and mechanize the metatheory in Lean 4 with zero sorry axioms.

2611.15146.title: Reframing Video Inverse Tone Mapping as Blind Posterior Inference via Latent Luminance Supervision
2611.15146.authors: Hanwool Sul, Chang-Hoon Jeong, Kisung Shin, Bomseok Park, Donghoon Cha, Hansl von Kwon, DoHyung Ku, Byoung-Tak Zhang
2611.15146.abstract: High-dynamic-range (HDR) displays are now common, but most video content, such as archival footage, broadcast material, and the output of generative video models, exists only in standard dynamic range (SDR). The need is sharpest for generated video, which has no HDR master at all and is graded alongside live-action and visual-effects material finished in HDR. Converting SDR to HDR means undoing a tone-mapping operation that was never recorded, and clipping destroys the radiance wherever it acts, so HDR recovery is a blind inverse problem. Methods built on generative video priors fill clipped regions with plausible structure, but their reconstructions are systematically biased: in every public method we test, saturated content leans too bright or too dark, and the direction of the lean moves with the tone operator behind the input. We call this failure the luminance error, measure both its magnitude and its sign, and make it the focus of this work. Reframing ITM as posterior inference under an unknown operator locates the failure in two places and yields two corrections. A fixed affine functional of the video-diffusion latent reads log-luminance without decoding; on that coordinate an asymmetric loss selects an expectile of the posterior, applied only where clipping leaves luminance unconstrained. We also synthesize training SDR through an explicit family of tone operators, so the model marginalizes over what the observation cannot show. Trained this way, our luminance error stays flatter across operators and smaller on average than any public method, and the full system achieves the best perceptual quality on all three benchmarks.

2611.16013.title: Runtime Analysis of Cartesian Genetic Programming on Max: A Proven Exponential Speedup
2611.16013.authors: Duc-Cuong Dang, Roman Kalkreuth, Andre Opris
2611.16013.abstract: Genetic Programming (GP) is a search paradigm inspired from natural evolution for the automated discovery of expressions, functions, and computer programs. Cartesian GP (CGP) is a flavor of GP that uses a graph-based model to encode candidate programs, as contrasted to the conventional Tree-based GP (TGP). Since its inception two decades ago, CGP has predominantly been analyzed empirically, thus little is known regarding its theoretical performance guarantees. This paper analyzes CGP for the Max problem, which has been only rigorously studied for TGP with a proven expected runtime superlinear in the optimal program length $n$. We prove that the expected time for the ($1$+$1$) CGP employing common mutation operators to evolve an equivalent optimal of the same output is polylogarithmic in $n$, specifically at most $O(\log^9{n})$. This is remarkable, as it shows an exponential speedup by switching to CGP. Our results shed light on the benefit and the compactness of the graph-based representation for programs, and on how CGP can navigate its search and fitness spaces efficiently. This is a first proven performance guarantee for CGP on an established benchmark problem. Experiments complement our theoretical findings.

2611.16057.title: Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads
2611.16057.abstract: Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.

2611.16424.title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning
2611.16424.authors: Haofeng Wang, Xuanyi Liu, Pengcheng Wen, Ruiqi Li, Yuhao Zhang, Tiange Zhang, Boren Zheng, Siyu Tao, Danni Yu, Gan Lin, Haocheng Tang, Tianzizhe Guo, Mingyuan Su, Boyuan Chen, Zhongyuan Wang
2611.16424.abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

2611.16726.title: From Data to Wisdom: Rethinking AI Through an Epistemic Lens
2611.16726.abstract: This paper proposes the Data-to-Wisdom Epistemic Architecture for AI (EAAI), a conceptual framework treating Data, Information, Knowledge, Understanding and Wisdom as five distinct but recursively interacting epistemic functions: observation, contextual interpretation, modeling and prediction, critical evaluation and informed judgment. Two observations motivate it: sequential readings of the Knowledge Pyramid obscure how these functions interact, and a targeted review of twelve Bayesian reference books finds that prior distributions are defined mathematically while "prior information" and "prior knowledge" are not consistently distinguished as epistemic categories. A Bayesian interpretation relates the likelihood, prior and posterior distributions, posterior prediction, model checking and decision analysis to the five functions, without limiting EAAI to Bayesian systems. Extending "prior" in an epistemic sense, the paper distinguishes five kinds of prior context that can shape the model, the likelihood, the prior, evaluation and action. Three worked applications -- quantitative financial risk, actuarial modeling in health insurance and agentic AI for medical reimbursement claims -- show how EAAI structures the analysis of model assumptions, evidence interpretation, validation, dependencies and decision consequences, separating the prediction of a risk, the appraisal of its reliability and the justification of action. It draws implications for AI and machine learning, including evaluation by function, treating intermediate model outputs as evidence open to challenge and separating generation from appraisal, and compares EAAI with work on DIKW, Bayesian workflow, AI evaluation and risk governance. Its contributions are an epistemic vocabulary with recursive relationships, a more accessible reading of Bayesian methodology, a typology of prior context and clearer methodological terminology

2611.16748.title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
2611.16748.authors: Yuxuan Chen, Xiaojie Li, Hao Chen, Juncheng Ma, Kewei Zhang, Zhongjing Du, Guoqiang Wei, Fangfang Wang, Zhen Dong, Zhiyang Dou, Liming Zhao, Yan Zeng, Jianwei Zhang, Daquan Zhou
2611.16748.abstract: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

2611.17048.title: Beyond Answering: Learning to Speak First and Act in Streaming Video
2611.17048.authors: Shuhan Li, Huankang Guan, Xintong Guo, Yang Bo, Yuyang He, Dunyuan Xu, Jingyan Chen, Fang Liu, Tsz Kin Wan, Jinpeng Chen, Zhenqi He, Yuxuan Hu, Wenbo Li, Han Gao, Qijun Li, Long Chen, Hongsheng Li, Rui Liu
2611.17048.abstract: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) lets the model act on what it sees by invoking external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporating returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities.

2611.17110.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
2611.17110.authors: Jiachun Jin, Zetong Zhou, Haonan Wang, Zhijie Deng
2611.17110.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.

2611.17442.title: Racing the Clock: Teaching VLNs Budget-Conditioned Object Search
2611.17442.authors: Maitree Meher, Siming He, S. Shankar Sastry, Jitendra Malik, Claire Tomlin, Jonas Frey
2611.17442.abstract: How do action budgets shape vision-language navigation (VLN) exploration, and what expert supervision best teaches budget-aware search? We study budget-conditioned object search: finding as many distinct instances of a requested category as possible within a budget, with discovery defined geometrically by camera field of view and proximity. Distinct discoveries provide a denser evaluation signal than single-target success. We cast expert design as a choice of scene abstraction: a single budget-indexed Bellman recursion, applied to different abstractions of the full environment, yields experts that differ in what they know. An object-level Bellman expert is given every target location and reduces search to budgeted routing. A room-level Bellman expert retains observed room connectivity, doorway evidence, and cross-scene semantic priors but withholds the contents of unexplored rooms, so it must search for targets that its student also cannot see. We distill both experts into Uni-NaVid under matched training conditions and also evaluate greedy-frontier supervision on held-out HM3D scenes. Changing only the stated budget changes learned trajectories. Despite higher object-level expert return, room-level supervision achieves the highest mean collection among evaluated VLNs at every tested budget. At 2000 steps, it finds 72.7% of reachable targets, versus 68.5% under greedy-frontier supervision, 65.5% under object-level supervision, and 44.8% for the pretrained VLN. These results show that expert-return rankings need not predict supervision quality for VLN exploration, and motivate choosing an expert's abstraction with the student's information in mind rather than by expert return alone.

2611.17466.title: Use-case-driven ontology modeling with the NeOn methodology for ambient assisted living
2611.17466.authors: Daniele Spoladore, Marco Sacco, Alberto Trombetta, Edoardo Battisti Sironi
2611.17466.abstract: Research on smart homes and ambient assisted living (AAL) has grown steadily over the last decade, driven largely by the ageing of the population. A smart home has to coordinate heterogeneous smart objects in order to offer services tailored to its dwellers, and this requires a shared formal description of both the dwellers and the devices. We present the ontology developed as the semantic data layer of the Virtual Home Framework in the Italian Design For All project. Its requirements are derived from two use cases: a frail elderly woman who exercises at home on a cycle-ergometer, and a designer who configures a kitchen for users with different impairments. The requirements are collected in an Ontology Requirements Specification Document and the ontology is built with the NeOn methodology, reusing and reengineering existing ontologies where possible. The resulting modular ontology describes users through the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and through their cardiorespiratory fitness; it also describes smart objects, their programs, the measurements they produce, and the comfort dimensions of the home. SWRL rules classify fitness levels, suggest exercise loads, assess indoor comfort, and identify the smart objects suited to a given impairment.

2611.17505.title: Adversarial Tracking: Attacks on Image Sensors for Object Tracking in Autonomous Vehicles
2611.17505.authors: Han Wu, Alex Chan, Ekin Can Erkus, Tousif Rahman, Rishad Shafik
2611.17505.abstract: Object Tracking systems estimate the motion of surrounding vehicles by linking detected objects across video frames. In particular, Tracking-By-Detection (TBD) systems combine object detectors with motion prediction and data association to maintain object identities over time. However, neural network-based detectors are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb input images, and their impact on downstream trajectory estimation is not fully characterized by detection accuracy alone. Therefore, this paper evaluates image-specific and image-agnostic attacks on YOLOv3 and YOLOv4 detectors paired with SORT, Deep SORT, Strong SORT, and OC-SORT tracking systems. The evaluation uses a CARLA autonomous driving simulator and measures tracking quality through Multiple Object Tracking Accuracy (MOTA), Higher Order Tracking Accuracy (HOTA) and Identification F1 (IDF1). Under image-specific attacks, HOTA for YOLOv3-based trackers declines from 53.45-56.19% to 14.85-17.03%, while MOTA reaches -772.60% in the worst case. YOLOv4-based trackers exhibit greater robustness, while HOTA still declines to 25.06-26.86%. In addition, image-agnostic attacks can reduce the tracking accuracy using a single Universal Adversarial Perturbation (UAP), without generating a separate perturbation for individual frames.

2611.18099.title: Eco3R: Pinned-Key Inference for Efficient and Streamable Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction from Long Videos
2611.18099.authors: Hongsen Cao, Shanxin Yuan, Mona Jaber, Ahmed Sayed
2611.18099.abstract: Feed-forward multi-view transformers such as VGGT recover the cameras and geometry of a video in one pass, but the cost of their cross-frame self-attention grows quadratically with the frame count, and their accuracy drops on long videos. Most remedies approximate attention over all frames under a fixed computational budget or select a few keys by their content. We hypothesize that the keys of a long video can be selected independently of video content, and our experiments on VGGT and $\pi^3$ support it: a small number of uniformly sampled frames can serve as the keys of every frame. We present Eco3R, a training-free inference framework whose keys form a Pinned Key Set of 31 such frames. A pin pass stores their tokens in a Scene Cache, and the other frames read it in independent batches that reproduce joint inference with these keys exactly, at a constant cost per frame. An Online Stream updates the pinned frames during recording. Six middle global blocks align the frames and form a reusable VGGT module: the Alignment Score reads their attention to flag failures, and Alignment Refocusing reduces them by fine-tuning only these blocks (3.6 GPU hours). Eco3R ($\pi^3$) matches $\pi^3$'s success rate on 1,000-frame ScanNet videos while running 13.8 times faster. With refocusing, Eco3R (VGGT) raises VGGT's success rate from 70% to 82% while running 8.5 times faster on 500 frames. Eco3R can reconstruct sequences of up to 4,000 frames on a single A100 GPU, while Eco3R ($\pi^3$) streams 1,000 frames at 18.6 fps, achieving the lowest online absolute trajectory error.
